key: Now these are the generations of Aaron and Moses in the day that the LORD spoke with Moses in mount Sinai.
s: Turning from the tribes’ census to Levi, the verses that follow name only Aaron’s sons; Rashi, on 3:1, reads them as Moses’ offspring too, since whoever teaches another’s son Torah is as if he begot him, and Ramban, on 3:1, by the plain sense, as Aaron’s alone, with Moses’ own sons counted among the Amramites.

evidence.gloss: [Rashi, on 3:1:] Yet it mentions only the sons of Aaron, and they are called the generations of Moses because he taught them Torah: this teaches that whoever teaches his fellow’s son Torah, Scripture accounts it to him as if he had begotten him. … [Ramban, on 3:1, after quoting Rashi:] By the plain sense, ‘the generations of Aaron and Moses’ means that the sons of Aaron were anointed priests, set apart from the tribe to be most holy, and the generations of Moses are the family of the Amramites which it mentions below … for among the Amramites none but Moses’ sons are counted with the Levites.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref Numbers 3:1, at [119,1] match). Plain sense faithful: the census of the tribes (chapters 1 to 2) gives way to Levi, and 3:2 to 4 name only Aaron’s sons. Rashi on 3:1: only Aaron’s sons are named, yet they are called Moses’ offspring because he taught them Torah, whoever teaches his fellow’s son Torah being accounted as if he begot him. Ramban on 3:1 quotes Rashi, then by the plain sense takes the generations of Aaron as his anointed sons and the generations of Moses as the Amramite family below, since only Moses’ sons are counted there among the Levites. Ramban closes by allowing the midrash as a hint of the text; the sentence limits his reading to “by the plain sense”, which is his own framing, so it does not overstate the difference. Ibn Ezra, Rashbam and Sforno read and do not conflict. entry-check ok.
